questions.stem: When we use a hash table data structure, our hash function should map the expected inputs (keys) as evenly as possible over its output range(indexes). This property of good hash function is known as______.
questions.hint: Trace the initial state and each executed operation in order, preserving the requested output layout.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 12

answer.explanation: DSA25 defines uniformity as spreading expected keys evenly among addresses. That directly matches the question’s wording. Determinism is a different obligation: repeated equal keys receive the same address for the chosen function. Continuity and data normalization do not name this distribution property, so only Uniformity answers the literal stem.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Uniformity describes spreading expected input keys evenly across the output address range, exactly as the stem requires.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Determinism requires repeated equal keys to map identically; it does not require an even address distribution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Continuity is not the key-distribution property defined for hash functions in DSA25.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Data normalization does not name the even-distribution requirement of a hash function.

evidence.quote: Determinism means repeated equal keys get the same address for the chosen function. Uniformity means expected keys spread evenly. Universal hashing chooses one function randomly from a suitable family for the table, independently of a fixed key set; it does not choose a fresh unrelated function for each lookup. Random choice controls collision probability, not a promise of zero collisions.

questions.stem: In a one-based array representation of a binary heap, the root is at index 1. If a node at index i has a right child, at which index is that child stored?
questions.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 13

answer.explanation: Heap child formulas depend on whether indexing begins at zero or one. With the explicitly stated one-based convention, the two children of node i occupy positions 2i and 2i+1. The latter is the right child. Integer division by two instead identifies a parent in this convention. The existence condition matters because an index computed beyond the current heap size does not designate an actual child.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 2i+1 is the one-based right-child index.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: floor(i/2) computes the parent for nonroot nodes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: (i+1)/2 does not compute the right child.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 2i is the one-based left child.

evidence.quote: Zero-based array representation: root index 0, left=2i+1, right=2i+2, parent=floor((i-1)/2) for i>0. One-based representation uses children 2i,2i+1 and parent floor(i/2). A child exists only if its index is inside the current heap size.

questions.stem: Use iterative sequential search and iterative binary search on random-access arrays, with constant-size indices. For binary search, reverse comparisons on descending arrays. Compare tight asymptotic auxiliary space and worst-case element probes as n grows. Which statement is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Binary searching algorithm can work on list of data which is stored in descending order

options.label: B
options.text: Sequential and binary searching algorithm are not equal in terms of memory efficiency

options.label: C
options.text: Sequential searching algorithm can work on sorted and unsorted list of data

options.label: D
options.text: Binary search has a smaller tight worst-case probe order than sequential search on sorted random-access arrays.

questions.hint: Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 14

answer.text: B. Sequential and binary searching algorithm are not equal in terms of memory efficiency
answer.explanation: Both iterative algorithms keep only a fixed number of indices and temporary values, giving constant auxiliary space. Their worst-case probe counts differ: sequential search can inspect every element, whereas binary search halves the ordered interval each time. Binary search can also handle descending order with reversed comparisons, and sequential search does not require sorted input. Under these specified implementations, the unequal-memory claim is the false statement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Descending binary search works with reversed comparisons.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Both iterative implementations use constant auxiliary space, so this inequality claim is false.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A sequential scan works with either input ordering.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Binary search has logarithmic rather than linear worst-case probes.

evidence.quote: Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted. Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too. A first-element match costs Theta(1). An absent target or last-position match needs n comparisons, giving Theta(n) worst time. Uniformly likely successful positions average (n+1)/2 comparisons, still linear.

Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.

questions.stem: For ordinary array sorting implementations, which listed algorithm uses a temporary element buffer proportional to n rather than only a fixed number of saved elements? Count recursive call frames separately from auxiliary element storage.
questions.hint: Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 45

answer.explanation: Ordinary array mergesort merges two sorted halves through a temporary buffer that can hold a number of elements proportional to n. Insertion sort retains one item while shifting, and selection sort needs fixed temporary storage for a minimum position and an exchange. Ordinary quicksort partitions inside the original array. Its recursive stack is counted separately here, so the linear element-buffer requirement uniquely identifies mergesort.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Insertion saves one item and shifts within the same array.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selection retains a minimum position and a fixed-size swap temporary.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary array merging needs a linear auxiliary element buffer.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: In-array partitioning needs no full merge buffer; recursive frames are excluded by the stated convention.

evidence.quote: Ordinary array merging needs a linear auxiliary buffer.
For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap.
At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i].
Quicksort normally rearranges in the same array but recursive storage can be linear in the worst case.

module_refs.title: Data Structure and Algorithms module

ii. Quick sort: is the fastest known algorithm. It uses divide and conquer strategy and in
the worst case its complexity is O (n2). But its expected complexity is O(nlogn).
Algorithm:
1. Choose a pivot value (mostly the first element is taken as the pivot value)
2. Position the pivot element and partition the list so that:
 the left part has items less than or equal to the pivot value
 the right part has items greater than or equal to the pivot value
3. Recursively sort the left part
4. Recursively sort the right part

module_refs.title: Data Structure and Algorithms module

Merge sort uses divide and conquer strategy and its time complexity is O(nlogn).
Algorithm:
1. Divide the array in to two halves.
2. Recursively sort the first n/2 items.
3. Recursively sort the last n/2 items.
4. Merge sorted items (using an auxiliary array).

questions.stem: An unsorted singly linked list maintains only its head pointer. Which option gives the complete set of listed operations with tight worst-case constant time? There is no cached tail, predecessor index or positional index.

options.label: A
options.text: Insertion at the front of the linked list

options.label: B
options.text: Insertion at the end of the linked list

options.label: C
options.text: Deletion of the front node of the linked list

options.label: D
options.text: Deletion of the last node of the linked list

questions.hint: Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage.
sources: Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 50

answer.explanation: Inserting at the head links the new node to the old head and updates head. Deleting the head advances head and releases one node. Both use constant work. Appending requires traversal to find the tail, and deleting the tail requires its predecessor, also found by traversal. The complete constant-time set is therefore insertion at the front together with deletion of the front, which is option E.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Front insertion is constant, but this alone omits the also-constant front deletion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Head-only append traverses the list to find its tail.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Front deletion is constant, but this alone omits the also-constant front insertion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Tail deletion must locate its predecessor by traversal.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: This combines exactly the two listed constant-time operations.

evidence.quote: Prepend with new.next=head; head=new. To insert after a known predecessor p, set new.next=p.next before p.next=new. Appending with only head requires a tail traversal; maintaining tail avoids it. Delete the head by saving old=head, advancing head=head.next and releasing old in C++.

Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires its predecessor, even when tail itself is known. Handle empty and single-node lists separately; after removing the only node, set both head and tail to null. To remove a known successor, bypass it before deallocation. Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node.

questions.stem: A capacity-six circular queue uses all six slots with front=0 and size=6. Its physical array is [11,13,15,17,19,21]. After dequeue() and enqueue(9), what is the logical front-to-rear sequence?
questions.hint: Trace the initial state and each executed operation in order, preserving the requested output layout.
sources: Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 55

answer.explanation: The initial front element is 11, so dequeue removes it and advances front to the slot containing 13. The queue now has five items. Circular insertion reuses the freed physical slot zero for 9 and restores size six. Reading from the new front around to the rear gives 13,15,17,19,21,9. Physical slot order differs from this requested logical service order.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This would remove 21 and prepend 9 rather than remove the front.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the front-to-rear order after removing 11 and appending 9.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This incorrectly retains 11 and removes the rear 21.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Circular reuse makes room for the insertion after the removal.

evidence.quote: A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.

questions.stem: Binary search is to operate on an already ordered sequence of comparable keys through an indexed-access interface. Which listed property is required of its search domain, rather than being a particular physical array representation or allocation policy?

options.label: A
options.text: The array must hold elements of the same data type.

options.label: D
options.text: The search interval must have valid finite bounds.

options.label: E
options.text: The array must fix its size a prior to population.

questions.hint: Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.
sources: Mock exam 4 · Question 19

answer.text: D. The search interval must have valid finite bounds.
answer.explanation: Binary search maintains an interval of candidate indices and repeatedly shrinks it until a match or an empty interval is obtained. That operation requires valid finite bounds. Homogeneous physical storage and contiguity are properties of ordinary array representations, rather than requirements of the abstract interval-halving procedure. Fixing capacity before population is unnecessary: a resizable sequence can be populated first and searched afterward. Hence not all listed properties are requirements.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Comparable keys are assumed; identical physical data types are not the abstract domain requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: All fails because prior fixed allocation is unnecessary.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Contiguity is a representation choice rather than the abstract search-domain requirement.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The candidate index domain needs valid finite bounds.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: A resizable sequence may be populated before searching.

choices.label: F
choices.explanation: Valid finite bounds are a required condition among these choices.

evidence.quote: On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. A queue retrieves the oldest entry first, while a linked list alone describes storage links without prescribing the needed access policy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A queue uses first-in, first-out access.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].

To evaluate postfix, push operands. At a binary operator, pop right operand first, then left, and push left op right. Build an expression tree for either prefix (preorder) or postfix (postorder); a stack is useful but is not the only possible conversion representation.

answer.explanation: Correctness asks whether operations produce their specified results. Time and space complexity measure operation counts and memory use under a resource model. evidence.quote: Binary means at most two children. Full means each node has zero or two children. Complete means all earlier levels are filled and the last fills from left. Perfect means all leaves share a level and every internal node has two children. Balanced means height stays logarithmic under a stated rule; it does not require a perfect shape.

Correctness means meeting the stated result for every valid input. A finite program can still return the wrong answer.

answer.explanation: An ordinary queue supplies exactly the stated FIFO operations: insertion at the rear and removal at the front. evidence.quote: An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served. answer.text: A. Bubble sort; D. Merge sort

Standard selection sort can reverse ties through a distant minimum exchange, and ordinary quicksort partitioning does not guarantee stable order. module_refs.title: Data Structure and Algorithms module
module_refs.quote:
iii. Heap Sort
Heap sort operates by first converting the list in to a heap tree. Heap tree is a binary tree in which
each node has a value greater than both its children (if any). It uses a process called "adjust to
accomplish its task (building a heap tree) whenever a value is larger than its parent. The time
complexity of heap sort is O(nlogn).
Algorithm:
1. Construct a binary tree
 The root node corresponds to Data[0].
 If we consider the index associated with a particular node to be i, then the left child of
this node corresponds to the element with index 2*i+1 and the right child corresponds
to the element with index 2*i+2. If any or both of these elements do not exist in the
array, then the corresponding child node does not exist either.
2. Construct the heap tree from initial binary tree using "adjust" process.
Sort by swapping the root value with the lowest, right most value and deleting the lowest, right
most value and inserting the deleted value in the array in it proper position.

evidence.quote: On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.

Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.

answer.explanation: Binary limits a node to at most two children; it does not require every node to have exactly two. The specified distinct-key model also requires uniqueness. Strict subtree ordering places every left-subtree key below its ancestor, so an equal key cannot appear there. A and C consequently hold under the stated model, while B and the all-of-the-above aggregate do not.

evidence.quote: Binary means at most two children. Full means each node has zero or two children. Complete means all earlier levels are filled and the last fills from left. Perfect means all leaves share a level and every internal node has two children. Balanced means height stays logarithmic under a stated rule; it does not require a perfect shape.

With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.

answer.text: Depth-first search uses a stack rather than the ordinary FIFO queue.
answer.explanation: DSA14 gives FIFO waiting, asynchronous buffers, and play sequences as queue uses. DSA42 explicitly contrasts DFS stack or recursion with a queue, which would change the discipline. This is a queue application, but it does not imply that every interrupt system uses a single FIFO service policy.

FIFO suits equal-priority printer jobs, shared-resource waiting, asynchronous buffers and level-order exploration. A play sequence can also use a queue. Distinguish airline seat records from waiting requests; an application name alone does not force one representation.

answer.explanation: Stacks support reversal by popping items in reverse insertion order. They also manage nested recursive calls and backtracking through the most recent pending context or choice. The stated asynchronous-transfer contract instead requires older buffered items to be delivered before newer arrivals. That is FIFO service, so an ordinary queue supplies the needed ordering. evidence.quote: Calls nest on a runtime stack; the latest call returns first. Bracket matching pushes opening brackets and matches each closing bracket against top. DFS and backtracking use the same latest-pending-choice discipline.

answer.text: A. Height-balanced BST; E. Sorted random-access array with binary search
answer.explanation: A height-balanced BST has logarithmic height, so following its ordered search path takes logarithmic worst-case time. answer.explanation: All left-subtree keys precede the root, and all right-subtree keys follow it. Recursively visiting left, parent, right therefore emits increasing keys. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 9.

evidence.quote: With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.

questions.stem: A fixed-capacity circular array queue uses front and size indices, modulo slot reuse, and no shifting or resizing. Under unit-cost index arithmetic, what is the tightest listed worst-case pair for enqueue and dequeue, including full/empty checks?
questions.hint: Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam · Sene 2016 · Question 27-1
Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 141

answer.explanation: Enqueue computes a slot from front and size, writes one item and updates the count. Dequeue reads the front slot, advances front modulo capacity and decreases the count. Full or empty checks also inspect only constant-size state. No operation shifts or resizes the array, so each uses constant work in the stated model. The linear alternatives are looser bounds rather than the requested tight pair.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear enqueue is looser than the constant cost of this implementation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Linear dequeue is looser than its constant index update cost.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both endpoint operations use constant work.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Both linear bounds are looser than the requested tight pair.

evidence.quote: A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.

Dequeue reads A[front], sets front=(front+1)%C and decreases size. An alternative reserves one unused slot and uses next(rear)==front for full; its empty test and capacity differ. State the convention before tracing.

answer.explanation: The global left-smaller/right-larger invariant defines the binary search tree family. It applies to every descendant in each subtree, not only immediate children. AVL and red-black trees satisfy that ordering but impose additional balancing disciplines, so they are more specialized than the family requested. The binary-tree restriction also excludes a general B-tree. Asking for the most general family prevents those BST subclasses from becoming competing selections.

evidence.quote: With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.

AVL balance factor is height(left)-height(right); every node must have factor -1,0 or 1. After insertion or deletion, update heights upward and rotate where necessary. LL imbalance needs a right rotation; RR needs left; LR rotates the left child left then the node right; RL is symmetric. Rotations preserve inorder key order.

A B-tree is a balanced multiway search tree. Its allowed branching factor can exceed two, so a general B-tree is not the binary-tree family. Balanced describes a height discipline; it does not by itself restrict every node to two children.

questions.stem: A bounded FIFO buffer must reuse freed array slots by wrapping indices modulo its fixed capacity, without shifting items. New insertions are rejected while full. Which listed term specifically names this storage representation?
questions.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 433

answer.explanation: A circular buffer reuses its fixed slots by wrapping indices modulo capacity, so released positions can be used again without moving surviving items. The FIFO order is tracked logically rather than by requiring the front to remain at physical slot zero. Queue names the service ADT and can have other representations; it does not specifically identify this layout. Stack and linked list likewise do not name the stated circular-array representation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A stack names LIFO service rather than the specified FIFO ring storage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Queue names the FIFO ADT but does not specifically identify its storage layout.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A linked list does not name modulo-indexed circular array slots.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Circular buffer specifically names the stated fixed-slot wraparound representation.

evidence.quote: A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.

Merging FIFO queues needs an explicit policy: append one sequence after another or alternate their fronts. Splitting by a predicate preserves each subgroup’s original order if each removed item is appended to its matching output queue. A fixed-capacity buffer also needs a full-policy choice: reject, block or overwrite. Capacity alone does not choose a policy.

Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 444

answer.text: B. Quick sort; C. Insertion sort
answer.explanation: Repeated extreme partitions make ordinary quicksort accumulate quadratic work. Insertion sort on reverse input similarly accumulates quadratic prefix shifts. Buffered mergesort and iterative heapsort have n log n worst-case bounds instead, so they are not tightly quadratic even though quadratic is a valid looser upper bound. The explicit tight-bound question therefore selects quicksort and insertion alone in this primary option set.

Reverse order causes 1+2+…+(n-1) shifts: quadratic time.
There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.
Building with bottom-up sinking is linear; repeated extraction gives O(n log n) worst time.

ii. Quick sort: is the fastest known algorithm. It uses divide and conquer strategy and in
the worst case its complexity is O (n2). But its expected complexity is O(nlogn).
Algorithm:

2. Position the pivot element and partition the list so that:
 the left part has items less than or equal to the pivot value
 the right part has items greater than or equal to the pivot value
3. Recursively sort the left part
4. Recursively sort the right part

The most instinctive type of sorting algorithm; it finds the location for an element and move all

item to the relatively sorted portion and find its correct location

module_refs.quote:
iv. Merge sort
Merge sort uses divide and conquer strategy and its time complexity is O(nlogn).
Algorithm:
1. Divide the array in to two halves.
2. Recursively sort the first n/2 items.
3. Recursively sort the last n/2 items.
4. Merge sorted items (using an auxiliary array).

module_refs.title: Data Structure and Algorithms module
module_refs.quote:
iii. Heap Sort
Heap sort operates by first converting the list in to a heap tree. Heap tree is a binary tree in which
each node has a value greater than both its children (if any). It uses a process called "adjust to
accomplish its task (building a heap tree) whenever a value is larger than its parent. The time
complexity of heap sort is O(nlogn).
Algorithm:
1. Construct a binary tree
 The root node corresponds to Data[0].
 If we consider the index associated with a particular node to be i, then the left child of
this node corresponds to the element with index 2*i+1 and the right child corresponds
to the element with index 2*i+2. If any or both of these elements do not exist in the
array, then the corresponding child node does not exist either.
2. Construct the heap tree from initial binary tree using "adjust" process.
Sort by swapping the root value with the lowest, right most value and deleting the lowest, right
most value and inserting the deleted value in the array in it proper position.

out the smallest or largest element to its proper position.

questions.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.

answer.explanation: Mergesort divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts them and merges their results, so it uses divide and conquer. Ordinary bubble sort uses adjacent passes and selection sort repeatedly selects a suffix minimum. The explicitly specified LSD radix method performs stable digit passes rather than recursive subproblem decomposition. This convention removes the possible confusion with MSD radix grouping while retaining the original primary answer.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The specified iterative LSD form uses digit passes rather than recursive divide and conquer.

evidence.quote: Divide and conquer reduces a problem to smaller instances of the same kind, solves the required smaller instances and obtains the original result from them. Mergesort recursively sorts two halves and merges; quicksort partitions and recursively sorts the resulting ranges. This course also classifies binary search as divide and conquer: an ordered comparison selects the only half that can contain the target. This is different from simply repeating adjacent swaps, choosing successive minima, or making stable LSD digit passes.

LSD radix sorting handles fixed-width digit keys by stably sorting least-significant digit first, then moving left. Stable intermediate passes preserve the ordering already established by less-significant digits. With d digits and radix r, counting-based passes take O(d(n+r)) time and O(n+r) auxiliary storage.
Begin with the first element already sorted. For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap.

variants.stem: Which ordinary sorting algorithms use divide and conquer by recursively sorting smaller subproblems? Select all that apply.

answer.text: B. Quick sort; C. Merge sort
answer.explanation: Quicksort partitions around a pivot and recursively sorts the smaller ranges. Top-down mergesort recursively sorts halves and merges their results. Both therefore apply divide and conquer. Bubble sort’s adjacent passes and ordinary insertion sort’s growing sorted prefix do not use this recursive subproblem decomposition. The complete answer is B and C; the question requires multiple selection.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sorting repeatedly swaps adjacent inversions instead of recursively decomposing subinstances.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort partitions around a pivot and recursively sorts the smaller ranges.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort recursively sorts halves and combines their sorted results.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ordinary insertion sort extends a sorted prefix instead of applying recursive divide and conquer.

evidence.quote: Divide and conquer reduces a problem to smaller instances of the same kind, solves the required smaller instances and obtains the original result from them. Mergesort recursively sorts two halves and merges; quicksort partitions and recursively sorts the resulting ranges. This course also classifies binary search as divide and conquer: an ordered comparison selects the only half that can contain the target. This is different from simply repeating adjacent swaps, choosing successive minima, or making stable LSD digit passes.

Choose a pivot, partition, then recursively sort the pieces. Balanced partitions give n log n work; repeated extreme pivots sum n+(n-1)+… to quadratic work. Expected n log n needs an input/random-pivot model. Random and median-of-three choices have different tradeoffs; neither is universally best.

Split into halves, sort them, then merge by advancing the smaller current front. With left-first tie handling, equal keys retain order. Ordinary array merging needs a linear auxiliary buffer. There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.
Begin with the first element already sorted. For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap.

questions.stem: Which specified sorting implementations preserve the relative order of equal full keys? Use ordinary in-place quicksort, ordinary heapsort, LSD radix with stable digit passes, and mergesort with left-first ties. Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 436

answer.text: C. Radix sort; D. Merge sort
answer.explanation: Stable LSD radix passes preserve the ordering already established by less significant digits. Equal full keys remain tied on every pass, so their relative order remains unchanged. Mergesort with left-first ties also preserves equal-key order while combining runs. Ordinary in-place quicksort and heapsort do not guarantee that stability because distant exchanges can reorder equal records. Hence both radix and merge qualify under the specified implementations.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Stable digit passes preserve the order of equal full keys.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Left-first merge ties preserve equal-key order.

module_refs.title: Data Structure and Algorithms module
module_refs.quote:
ii. Quick sort: is the fastest known algorithm. It uses divide and conquer strategy and in
the worst case its complexity is O (n2). But its expected complexity is O(nlogn).
Algorithm:
1. Choose a pivot value (mostly the first element is taken as the pivot value)
2. Position the pivot element and partition the list so that:
 the left part has items less than or equal to the pivot value
 the right part has items greater than or equal to the pivot value
3. Recursively sort the left part
4. Recursively sort the right part

module_refs.title: Data Structure and Algorithms module
module_refs.quote:
iii. Heap Sort
Heap sort operates by first converting the list in to a heap tree. Heap tree is a binary tree in which
each node has a value greater than both its children (if any). It uses a process called "adjust to
accomplish its task (building a heap tree) whenever a value is larger than its parent. The time
complexity of heap sort is O(nlogn).
Algorithm:
1. Construct a binary tree
 The root node corresponds to Data[0].
 If we consider the index associated with a particular node to be i, then the left child of
this node corresponds to the element with index 2*i+1 and the right child corresponds
to the element with index 2*i+2. If any or both of these elements do not exist in the
array, then the corresponding child node does not exist either.
2. Construct the heap tree from initial binary tree using "adjust" process.
Sort by swapping the root value with the lowest, right most value and deleting the lowest, right
most value and inserting the deleted value in the array in it proper position.

module_refs.title: Data Structure and Algorithms module
module_refs.quote:
iv. Merge sort
Merge sort uses divide and conquer strategy and its time complexity is O(nlogn).
Algorithm:
1. Divide the array in to two halves.
2. Recursively sort the first n/2 items.
3. Recursively sort the last n/2 items.
4. Merge sorted items (using an auxiliary array).

questions.stem:
Which searching algorithm is based on comparing the target value with elements at
midpoints of the array?
questions.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 439

answer.explanation: DSA29 computes the midpoint of the current ordered interval, compares it with the target, and discards the half that cannot contain the target. That is exactly the midpoint-based procedure in the stem. Linear search scans successive elements, interpolation estimates a position from values, and DFS follows graph branches rather than ordered-array midpoints.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search compares successive elements rather than repeatedly choosing the midpoint of a shrinking ordered interval.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search explicitly compares the target with the current interval midpoint and keeps one half.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Interpolation search estimates a probe from numeric values and their distribution, rather than always using the midpoint.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Depth-first search explores graph neighbors and branches, not ordered-array midpoint intervals.

evidence.quote: On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.

Interpolation search estimates the index from numeric values: lo+(hi-lo)×(key-A[lo])/(A[hi]-A[lo]), rounded to a valid index. Guard equal endpoints and out-of-range targets. On sorted, suitably uniform data its expected probes can be O(log log n); pathological distributions can require linear time. Binary search gives a logarithmic worst bound without that distribution assumption.

questions.stem: Which named algorithms explore a graph or tree by following adjacency links to unvisited vertices, using branch-first or distance-layer-first traversal? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 443

answer.text: C. Depth-first search; D. Breadth-first search
answer.explanation: DFS explores an unvisited branch before returning to later neighbors, using recursion or a stack. BFS instead processes a FIFO frontier so successive distance layers are explored in order. Both follow adjacency relationships and apply to trees as well as general graphs. Linear sequence scanning and binary interval search are different algorithms and do not implement these two adjacency-frontier traversal disciplines.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear sequence search does not implement the specified adjacency-frontier traversal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search eliminates ordered interval halves rather than following arbitrary adjacency.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DFS is branch-first adjacency traversal.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: BFS is distance-layer-first adjacency traversal.

evidence.quote: Mark the source when enqueuing it. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, examine its neighbours, and enqueue each unvisited neighbour while marking it. Store predecessor[v] when discovering v if a path must be reconstructed. FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers.

Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours. An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline. Marking prevents infinite repetition around graph cycles.

sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 461

answer.text: Merge sort using buffered external runs.
answer.explanation: DSA37 describes external sorting by building sorted runs and merging buffered disk streams to reduce I/O. Merge sort naturally supports that strategy even when the whole dataset does not fit RAM. Bubble and insertion sorting repeatedly move local data, while ordinary quicksort assumes partition access rather than the external sequential-run pattern specified here.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sort’s repeated adjacent passes do not provide the buffered sorted-run strategy used for efficient external sorting.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary quicksort partitioning is not the sequential buffered-run merging strategy identified for external data here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sorting combines buffered sorted runs sequentially and is directly suited to disk-backed external sorting.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion sort’s repeated local insertion work does not provide the note’s efficient external-run merging mechanism.

evidence.quote: Top-down mergesort recurses; bottom-up merges runs of widths 1,2,4,… iteratively. In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant. Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory. External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O. Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons.

Merge sort uses divide and conquer strategy and its time complexity is O(nlogn).

4. Merge sorted items (using an auxiliary array).

questions.stem: A large dataset has an equality-key index implemented by a hash table with suitable key distribution and bounded load. No ordered or range queries are needed. Which listed search uses this index for expected constant-time lookup?
questions.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 462

answer.explanation: Hash lookup computes a bucket or probe start from the key and uses the existing index to locate an equality match. With suitable distribution and bounded load, the note gives expected constant lookup. The important assumptions are the index and workload, rather than dataset size alone. Linear scanning ignores the index, binary search needs an ordered interval, and DFS follows graph relationships instead of this equality-key access structure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A scan can inspect linearly many records and does not use the hash index.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search uses an ordered interval rather than this index.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash search uses the stated index with expected constant lookup.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS follows graph connections rather than the equality-key index.

evidence.quote: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.

A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering. A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list. Move a hit to the recent end and evict the least-recent end when full. No storage structure is universally best without operation and policy requirements.

questions.stem: For a uniform random permutation of distinct keys, which listed ordinary algorithms have the smallest tight average-case growth order? Use fixed-position-pivot quicksort, buffered mergesort without merge-skipping, and standard bubble/insertion. Select all algorithms tied for the smallest order.
questions.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 463

answer.text: B. Quick sort; C. Merge sort
answer.explanation: Under the stated random-input model, ordinary quicksort has expected n log n work. Buffered mergesort performs n log n work in every order, so its average shares that order. Bubble and insertion have quadratic average work on random permutations. Quicksort and mergesort therefore tie for the smallest asymptotic average order among these options; the question does not ask for a measured running-time ranking between the tied methods. The DSA31 comparison table supplies the average-case entries used in this comparison.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Quadratic average growth is larger than n log n.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Expected n log n ties for the smallest listed average growth.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: n log n across orders ties for the smallest listed average growth.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Quadratic average growth is larger than n log n.

evidence.quote: n log n / n log n / n²
n / n² / n²
There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.

insertion?
questions.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 464

answer.text: Hash table for expected fast dictionary lookup and insertion.
answer.explanation: DSA27 explicitly names hashing as a dictionary implementation with expected constant lookup. DSA26 qualifies this by a suitable distribution and controlled load; insertion is likewise expected fast under those conditions. Arrays and linked lists lack the same ordinary key-lookup performance, while a stack specifies LIFO access. This is an expected-performance recommendation, not a universal worst-case guarantee.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An ordinary array lacks key-derived lookup and may require scanning or maintaining a sorted order with costly insertions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ordinary linked list needs traversal to locate an arbitrary dictionary key, giving linear worst-case lookup.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A well-sized hash table offers expected fast key lookup and insertion under suitable hashing and load assumptions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A stack exposes LIFO top operations and does not directly provide efficient arbitrary-key dictionary lookup.

evidence.quote: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.

A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering. A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list. Move a hit to the recent end and evict the least-recent end when full. No storage structure is universally best without operation and policy requirements.

questions.stem: Which listed algorithm guarantees shortest paths from one source to all reachable vertices for arbitrary graphs with nonnegative edge weights that may differ? Compare the standard forms of the listed algorithms.
questions.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 465

answer.explanation: Standard Dijkstra repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance and relaxes its outgoing edges. Nonnegative edge weights justify this shortest-path procedure even when different edges have different costs. BFS minimizes edge count and is sufficient when edge costs are equal, which is weaker than the stated guarantee. DFS supplies reachability paths, while Prim minimizes total spanning-tree cost rather than source-to-vertex route lengths.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A DFS path need not have minimum total weight.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: BFS minimizes edge count and does not guarantee minimum weight for arbitrary differing costs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dijkstra guarantees source shortest paths under nonnegative weights.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Prim solves the spanning-tree objective rather than source shortest paths.

evidence.quote: For nonnegative weights, standard Dijkstra initializes source distance zero and others infinity, repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with smallest distance, and relaxes each outgoing edge: dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w(u,v)). A min-priority queue supports the next choice. BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.
BFS finds minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary minimum-weight paths.

questions.stem: Which listed standard representations directly implement stack push/pop at an array top or linked-chain head, without simulating LIFO through another ADT? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 466

answer.explanation: The array representation maintains a top index and changes it when pushing or popping. The linked representation inserts and removes at the chain head, so the latest node is also the next one removed. Both directly implement LIFO with ordinary constant endpoint operations. A queue has FIFO service, while a generic tree has no stack-top contract; emulations through those ADTs are outside this representation question.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An array with a top index directly implements stack operations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A linked chain with head insertion/removal directly implements stack operations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An ordinary FIFO queue is not a direct stack representation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A generic tree does not supply the specified stack-top representation.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].
Arrays or linked nodes can implement the same LIFO stack.

questions.stem: Given a consistent comparator on a priority field, which listed comparison sorting algorithms can sort records by that field? No particular extraction mechanism or equal-priority stability is required. Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 467

answer.text: A. Bubble sort; B. Quick sort; C. Merge sort; D. Heap sort
answer.explanation: Priority is a key field that any comparison sort can use through a consistent comparator. Bubble compares neighboring priorities, quicksort partitions by priority, mergesort combines priority-ordered runs, and heapsort repeatedly places a priority extreme. Since no heap-extraction mechanism or tie-stability condition is required, every listed algorithm can produce the requested priority ordering. Priorities alone do not identify one unique sorting method.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble can compare adjacent priority fields.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort can partition with the priority comparator.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Mergesort can merge runs by the priority field.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Heapsort can extract priority extremes.

evidence.quote: It is not uniquely the method for sorting by priorities: any comparison sort can compare a priority field. Heap extraction is its distinctive mechanism.

iii. Heap Sort
Heap sort operates by first converting the list in to a heap tree. Heap tree is a binary tree in which
each node has a value greater than both its children (if any). It uses a process called "adjust to
accomplish its task (building a heap tree) whenever a value is larger than its parent. The time
complexity of heap sort is O(nlogn).
Algorithm:
1. Construct a binary tree
 The root node corresponds to Data[0].
 If we consider the index associated with a particular node to be i, then the left child of
this node corresponds to the element with index 2*i+1 and the right child corresponds
to the element with index 2*i+2. If any or both of these elements do not exist in the
array, then the corresponding child node does not exist either.
2. Construct the heap tree from initial binary tree using "adjust" process.
Sort by swapping the root value with the lowest, right most value and deleting the lowest, right
most value and inserting the deleted value in the array in it proper position.

questions.stem: An LRU cache already has hash lookup that returns a reference to the matching entry. Which listed representation should maintain recency order so a known entry can be removed and moved to the recent end in constant time, with eviction at the least-recent end?

options.label: B
options.text: Doubly linked list with head and tail

questions.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 468

answer.text: B. Doubly linked list with head and tail
answer.explanation: The hash index handles locating an entry, while the recency component must unlink a known entry and reconnect it at the recent end. A doubly linked list supplies both neighboring links for that constant-time removal and maintains endpoints for movement and eviction. An array would generally shift entries, a bare hash table does not supply recency order, and an ordinary FIFO queue cannot remove an arbitrary known interior entry.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Maintaining array recency order generally requires shifts.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A doubly linked recency list supports unlinking a known node and endpoint updates.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The existing hash index handles lookup but does not itself maintain LRU order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An ordinary queue lacks arbitrary known-interior-node removal.

evidence.quote: A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering. A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list. Move a hit to the recent end and evict the least-recent end when full. No storage structure is universally best without operation and policy requirements.

Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends. Singly linked tail deletion still needs its predecessor. A circular tail links back to head; stop traversal on returning to the start, handling empty separately.

questions.stem: Which algorithm is used to find the maximum subarray sum in an array?
questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 469

answer.explanation: DSA44 directly identifies Kadane as the contiguous maximum-sum-subarray algorithm. It updates the best sum ending at the current item and the best sum seen overall, using linear time and constant working storage. Binary search does not optimize contiguous sums, and quicksort or merge sort reorder values rather than preserve the original adjacency needed by this problem.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Binary search locates targets or ordered boundaries; it does not compute a contiguous maximum-sum subarray.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort reorders values and does not preserve the original adjacency required for maximum subarray sum.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort orders values; the named sorting algorithm is not the maximum-subarray recurrence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Kadane maintains the best sum ending here and the best anywhere, directly solving the stated problem.

evidence.quote: Kadane’s algorithm finds a contiguous maximum-sum subarray. For a required nonempty answer, initialize ending=best=A[0]; update ending=max(x,ending+x), then best=max(best,ending). It is linear time with constant working storage. Initializing best=0 instead silently allows an empty answer and fails the nonempty all-negative case.

questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

answer.explanation: DSA40 describes adjacency lists as storing each vertex’s neighbors in Θ(V+E) space. This names a complete graph representation among the choices. Arrays, linked lists, or maps may store parts of a representation, but those container names alone do not specify how vertices and their edges are encoded. The answer identifies the graph-specific organization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An array can store a matrix or adjacency containers, but its name alone does not specify a graph representation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A linked list can hold neighbor records, but alone does not describe the vertex-to-neighbor organization.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash tables may index vertices or neighbors, but do not by themselves name the graph representation supplied here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An adjacency list explicitly associates vertices with their neighbors and is a standard graph representation.

evidence.quote: A matrix uses Theta(V²) space and constant edge lookup. Adjacency lists use Theta(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours. Dense simple graphs approach quadratic edge counts. Examining every edge costs more on denser graphs; vertex-only operations need not inspect every edge.

questions.stem: Which algorithm is used to find the minimum spanning tree in a graph?
questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 471

answer.explanation: DSA43 defines an MST as a minimum-total-cost connection of all vertices in a connected undirected weighted graph. Prim repeatedly adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex. Dijkstra minimizes source-path distances instead, while BFS and DFS are traversals without a general minimum-weight spanning-tree guarantee. Thus Prim is the listed MST algorithm.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DFS can produce a spanning tree but does not generally minimize total edge weight.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: BFS produces minimum-edge source layers in unweighted graphs, not a general minimum-weight spanning tree.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dijkstra minimizes source-to-vertex distances, a different objective from total spanning-tree connection cost.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Prim grows a spanning tree by repeatedly choosing a cheapest edge crossing to an outside vertex.

evidence.quote: An MST minimizes the total cost of connecting all vertices of a connected undirected weighted graph. Prim adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex. Kruskal processes edges by increasing weight and rejects those joining vertices already connected. An MST need not give shortest source-to-vertex routes, and equal weights can permit several MSTs.

For nonnegative weights, standard Dijkstra initializes source distance zero and others infinity, repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with smallest distance, and relaxes each outgoing edge: dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w(u,v)). A min-priority queue supports the next choice. BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.

questions.stem: A priority queue needs O(1) peek and O(log n) worst-case insertion and extraction for an interleaved workload. Compare ordinary sorted/unsorted array and linked-list implementations, a binary heap, and an unmodified FIFO queue; exclude representations with extra search indexes. Which meets all requirements?
questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
sources: Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 472

answer.explanation: A binary heap exposes the extreme key at its root, so peek is constant, and insertion or extraction restores order along a logarithmic-height path. Ordinary unordered arrays or lists need a linear search for an extreme, while ordered versions pay linear insertion in the general case. An unmodified FIFO queue follows arrival order rather than priority. The stated operation bounds make the heap the unique matching standard representation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary ordered/unsorted arrays trade linear insertion against linear extremum selection.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary lists likewise have a linear cost in one required operation.

module_refs.quote:
iii. Heap Sort
Heap sort operates by first converting the list in to a heap tree. Heap tree is a binary tree in which
each node has a value greater than both its children (if any). It uses a process called "adjust to
accomplish its task (building a heap tree) whenever a value is larger than its parent. The time
complexity of heap sort is O(nlogn).
Algorithm:
1. Construct a binary tree
 The root node corresponds to Data[0].
 If we consider the index associated with a particular node to be i, then the left child of
this node corresponds to the element with index 2*i+1 and the right child corresponds
to the element with index 2*i+2. If any or both of these elements do not exist in the
array, then the corresponding child node does not exist either.
2. Construct the heap tree from initial binary tree using "adjust" process.
Sort by swapping the root value with the lowest, right most value and deleting the lowest, right
most value and inserting the deleted value in the array in it proper position.

answer.text: C. Hash table allocates one separate memory slot for each key in the universe U

choices.label: B

questions.stem:
Which method can resolve collision in hashed files by proceeding from the occupied position
specified by the hash address and checking subsequent positions until an empty position is found?
questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
sources: Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 133

answer.explanation: DSA26 defines open addressing as keeping entries within the array and probing until an available slot is found. Checking successive positions is its linear-probing form. Multiple hashing changes probe steps, chaining stores collisions in bucket lists, and cluster indexing is not this insertion procedure. Therefore Open addressing is the matching general method among the options.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Open addressing searches alternative table positions; checking successive positions is its linear-probing form.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Multiple or double hashing derives another probe step rather than the stated simple successive-slot scan.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Chaining puts colliding entries in a bucket list instead of searching successive array slots.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Cluster indexing does not name the collision insertion strategy described by the successive-position probing rule.

evidence.quote: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.

Linear probing tries (h(k)+j)%m. For size 7 and keys 10,17,24, all home addresses are 3 and occupied positions become 3,4,5. Quadratic probing changes the step; double hashing uses h1(k)+j h2(k), modulo m, with a step relatively prime to m to cover all slots. Neither method guarantees no collisions. Deletion needs tombstones or reinsertion so searches do not stop prematurely.

answer.explanation: The most recently pushed item is removed first by a stack. This is last in, first out, abbreviated LIFO. Equivalently, the first item inserted remains until later items have been removed, making it first in, last out or FILO. FIFO and FCFS instead preserve arrival order in ordinary queue service. Both A and C therefore name the same stack discipline.

An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served. answer.explanation: Binary search repeatedly removes roughly half of the remaining candidate interval. The note bounds its worst probes by floor(log₂n)+1 for nonempty input, giving logarithmic worst-case time under constant-cost indexing. The linear, quadratic and n-times-squared-log options all grow faster and are looser upper bounds. Explicitly asking for the tightest bound selects the logarithmic alternative rather than treating every valid Big-O upper bound as equally responsive.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quadratic is a looser upper bound.

choices.label: C

choices.explanation: Logarithmic matches the interval-halving probe growth.

evidence.quote: Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. evidence.quote: A C struct groups named fields, including arrays and pointers. A singly linked node needs payload plus a same-type link. C fields cannot have initializers inside the type declaration; modern C++ permits default member initializers. In C++, match new with delete and new[] with delete[]. Repair links before freeing a node; never dereference it afterwards.

Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires its predecessor, even when tail itself is known. Handle empty and single-node lists separately; after removing the only node, set both head and tail to null. To remove a known successor, bypass it before deallocation. Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node.

answer.explanation: For n≥1, 6n+4≤10n, while 6n+4≥6n. These constant upper and lower multiples establish linear growth by DSA06. O(n) is the natural tightest-order response, though larger upper bounds also exist.

evidence.quote: For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. Little-o means f/g tends to zero; little-omega means it grows without bound. These relations can describe best-case, average-case, worst-case or space functions.

answer.explanation: DSA04 defines finiteness as terminating after finitely many steps for every valid input. It is distinct from definiteness, executable instructions, or correctness: a terminating procedure can still return a wrong answer. The required concept is directly covered.

evidence.quote: Finiteness means termination after finitely many steps for every valid input. Definiteness means each instruction has one interpretation; effectiveness means each step is executable. questions.stem: An algorithm has exactly two independent nested loops. Each executes n iterations, and the innermost body performs constant work. Loop-control operations are constant time, with no early exits or hidden nonconstant operations. What is the tight time complexity as n grows?
questions.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 12

answer.explanation: For each of the n outer iterations, the inner loop executes n times, so the constant-cost body runs n×n=n² times. Outer-loop overhead is linear and inner-loop control is also bounded by a constant per body execution. Those contributions do not change the dominant quadratic growth. Under the stated independence, fixed loop count and body-cost assumptions, the tight time complexity is Theta(n²).

evidence.quote: A loop i=1; i<n; i*=2 takes about log₂n iterations. Two independent n-iteration loops nested around constant work take Theta(n²). An n-level ordinary recursion with constant live storage per level needs Theta(n) stack space.

Time counts chosen operations; space counts memory, including live recursive frames. Distributed algorithms may also measure communication volume. A single assignment is one unit in the elementary model, not literally one second. Sequential blocks add costs; independent nested loops multiply their iteration counts. Conditional worst-case cost includes the test and the more expensive branch.

answer.text: Both upper and lower asymptotic bounds.

It is independent of choosing best, average, or worst input cases; Average case only confuses the bound relation with an input-distribution choice.

evidence.quote: For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. questions.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of Linear Search and when does it occur?
questions.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 19

answer.text: Θ(n) worst time, when absent or at the last position.
answer.explanation: DSA28 scans until equality or exhaustion. An absent target or one in the final position requires all n comparisons, giving linear worst time; a first-position match instead takes constant time. The operation and cases are directly supported.

evidence.quote: Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted. Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too. A first-element match costs Theta(1). An absent target or last-position match needs n comparisons, giving Theta(n) worst time. Uniformly likely successful positions average (n+1)/2 comparisons, still linear.

questions.stem: Binary Search requires the list to be:
questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 20

answer.explanation: DSA29 eliminates half an ordered interval according to the midpoint comparison. That elimination is valid only when comparable values follow a consistent order; descending input works with reversed comparisons. Circularity and links are representation properties, not substitutes for sortedness. An unsorted sequence gives no safe smaller-half decision. Therefore Sorted is the required prerequisite.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Without order, a midpoint comparison cannot safely eliminate either half.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistent sorted order supports the midpoint half-elimination invariant.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Circular storage does not establish the value ordering needed by binary search.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Linked storage does not imply sortedness and also changes midpoint-access costs.

evidence.quote: On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.

questions.stem: How many steps does Binary Search take for a list of 1,000,000 elements (approximately)?

answer.explanation: DSA29 gives floor(log₂n)+1 probes for n>0. Since 2^19=524288 and 2^20=1048576, one million lies between them, so the worst probe count is twenty under the ordinary interval algorithm. A root/midpoint hit can finish earlier.

evidence.quote: Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.

questions.stem: What is the time complexity of Bubble Sort and why?
questions.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 22

answer.text: Worst and usual average Θ(n²); early-stop best Θ(n).
answer.explanation: DSA32 sums repeated adjacent passes to at most n(n−1)/2 comparisons, yielding quadratic worst and ordinary average work. A no-swap early-stop pass makes sorted input linear, while a fixed pass schedule remains quadratic. The answer needs these implementation and case distinctions.

evidence.quote: For ascending order, compare each adjacent pair and swap only when left>right. The largest remaining value moves to the final unsorted position after one left-to-right pass. Shrink the next pass by one position. Quadratic worst/average work comes from up to n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons.

questions.stem: In Selection Sort, what does each pass through the unsorted subarray accomplish?
questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 23

answer.text: Select the remaining minimum and put it at the next prefix position.
answer.explanation: DSA33 scans the unsorted suffix for its minimum and exchanges it with A[i]. After each meaningful pass, the sorted prefix grows by one and contains the smallest keys placed so far. This differs from inserting the next encountered item into a prefix.

evidence.quote: At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i]. There are n-1 meaningful placements and n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of initial order. At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed. A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls.

questions.stem: How does Insertion Sort differ from Selection Sort conceptually?
questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 24

answer.text: Selection finds a suffix minimum; insertion places the next item into a sorted prefix.
answer.explanation: DSA33 chooses the globally smallest remaining key for each next output position. DSA34 instead takes the next input item, shifts larger prefix values, and inserts it into their gap. Both grow sorted prefixes, but choose their next item differently.

evidence.quote: At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i]. There are n-1 meaningful placements and n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of initial order. At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed. A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls.

Begin with the first element already sorted. For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap. That gives n-1 insertion passes. On sorted input each pass needs one ordering check and no shifts: linear time. Reverse order causes 1+2+…+(n-1) shifts: quadratic time.

questions.stem: What is the best-case scenario for Bubble Sort and what is its complexity in that case?

sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 25

answer.text: Already sorted input; Θ(n) with no-swap early stopping.
answer.explanation: DSA32 performs one pass over an already sorted array, makes no swaps, and stops when early-exit detection is enabled. That is linear best work. A fixed-pass implementation still executes its quadratic comparison schedule even on the same input.

evidence.quote: Early stopping makes a sorted input linear: one no-swap pass finishes. A fixed pass schedule stays quadratic. Strict swaps preserve equal-key order. Cocktail sort runs bubble passes in both directions and is stable with strict swaps.

questions.stem: What are the two components of each node in a singly linked list?

answer.explanation: DSA08 defines a singly linked node as data plus next. The head reference points to the first node, and a null next terminates an ordinary noncircular chain. Head is a list-level reference rather than a second payload field inside every node.

evidence.quote: A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain. Empty means head==null. Nodes allocated as needed grow dynamically, with pointer overhead and no direct index arithmetic.

questions.stem: How does a circular linked list differ from a singly linked list?
