answer.text: A circular tail links back to head instead of ending at null.
answer.explanation: DSA10 defines circularity by the tail-to-head link and stops traversal after returning to the start. This is independent of singly versus doubly linked: a singly linked list can itself be circular. Compared with the ordinary noncircular singly linked chain, termination changes from null to return-to-start.

evidence.quote: Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends. Singly linked tail deletion still needs its predecessor. A circular tail links back to head; stop traversal on returning to the start, handling empty separately.

A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain. Empty means head==null. Nodes allocated as needed grow dynamically, with pointer overhead and no direct index arithmetic.

questions.stem: To delete a node from the front of a singly linked list, what single update is needed?
questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 28

answer.text: Advance head to the old head’s next link, then reclaim the old node.
answer.explanation: DSA09 saves old=head, sets head=head.next, and releases old in an owned C++ chain. The essential link update is advancing head; check empty before dereferencing, and clear tail too if the only node was removed. This answers the operation without hiding ownership work.

evidence.quote: Prepend with new.next=head; head=new. To insert after a known predecessor p, set new.next=p.next before p.next=new. Appending with only head requires a tail traversal; maintaining tail avoids it. Delete the head by saving old=head, advancing head=head.next and releasing old in C++.

Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires its predecessor, even when tail itself is known. Handle empty and single-node lists separately; after removing the only node, set both head and tail to null. To remove a known successor, bypass it before deallocation. Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node.

questions.stem: What extra pointer does each node in a doubly linked list have compared to a singly linked list?
questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

answer.text: A prev link to the predecessor.
answer.explanation: DSA10 says doubly linked nodes add prev alongside next. That extra link permits backward traversal and supports endpoint updates when head and tail are maintained. It does not automatically give constant arbitrary positional access, which may still need traversal.

evidence.quote: Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends. Singly linked tail deletion still needs its predecessor. A circular tail links back to head; stop traversal on returning to the start, handling empty separately.

questions.stem: Why do linked lists have slower access times than arrays?

sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 30

answer.text: Arrays compute addresses directly; linked positional access follows a chain.
answer.explanation: DSA02 computes an element address from base, index, and element size in constant time. DSA08’s chain lacks direct index arithmetic, so reaching an arbitrary position may traverse linearly many links. This comparison concerns positional access rather than every operation: a known-head update can be constant.

evidence.quote: For equal-size elements, address(A[i]) = base + i × element_size under zero-based indexing. This arithmetic gives constant-time positional access in the usual RAM cost model. A row-major rectangular matrix uses base + (row × columns + column) × element_size.

A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain. Empty means head==null. Nodes allocated as needed grow dynamically, with pointer overhead and no direct index arithmetic.

questions.stem: Convert the infix expression A + B * C - D / E to postfix.
questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 31

answer.explanation: DSA13 works the exact expression. Multiplication groups B*C and division groups D/E before addition and subtraction. Emit A, then B C *, then +, then D E /, then −, producing ABC*+DE/-.

evidence.quote: Infix places an operator between operands and uses precedence and parentheses. Prefix places it first; postfix places it last. Their fixed operator arity determines grouping. To convert infix to postfix, output operands immediately and hold operators on a stack. Pop higher-precedence operators before pushing a new operator; also pop equal precedence for left-associative operators. Parentheses temporarily override this order.
A+B*C-D/E becomes ABC*+DE/-.

questions.stem: What condition causes stack overflow in an array-implemented stack?
questions.hint: Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 32

answer.text: Attempting push when the fixed array is full.
answer.explanation: DSA11 distinguishes full storage from the overflow attempt. Under zero-based top-as-last-occupied convention, full means top=C−1; a count convention uses size=C. A push must check this before writing beyond capacity.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].
Overflow is an attempted insertion into full storage; underflow is an attempted removal from empty storage.

questions.stem: What are the three main operations of a Stack and their time complexities?
questions.hint: State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 33

answer.text: Push, pop, and peek are O(1) for fixed-array or head-linked stacks.
answer.explanation: DSA11 defines push insertion, pop removal/return, and peek observation at top. Fixed-array indexing and linked-head updates take constant work. A resizing append or singly linked tail-pop implementation can change the cost, so the guarantee needs the stated representations.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].

A count-based alternative uses size=0 and A[size++]=x. Do not combine its empty/full tests with the top-index convention. Fixed-array push/pop are constant time. Linked stacks achieve constant time by inserting and deleting at the head; using a singly linked tail for pop would require a predecessor traversal.

questions.stem: In postfix notation, why are parentheses unnecessary?

sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 34

answer.text: Operator position and known arity determine grouping.
answer.explanation: DSA13 places postfix operators after their operands. During stack evaluation, each binary operator consumes the two latest operand values in right-then-left order and pushes their result. The sequence therefore encodes grouping without precedence parentheses.

evidence.quote: Infix places an operator between operands and uses precedence and parentheses. Prefix places it first; postfix places it last. Their fixed operator arity determines grouping. To convert infix to postfix, output operands immediately and hold operators on a stack. Pop higher-precedence operators before pushing a new operator; also pop equal precedence for left-associative operators. Parentheses temporarily override this order.

To evaluate postfix, push operands. At a binary operator, pop right operand first, then left, and push left op right. Build an expression tree for either prefix (preorder) or postfix (postorder); a stack is useful but is not the only possible conversion representation.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a simple array queue and a circular queue?
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.

answer.text: Circular wraparound reuses freed front slots; a simple noncircular queue may not.
answer.explanation: DSA15 distinguishes a rear index reaching the array end from circular modulo arithmetic. A circular queue can insert into positions freed at the front, while a simple noncircular version may report overflow despite those gaps. Capacity and empty/full conventions still must be consistent.

evidence.quote: A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.

questions.stem: A stable priority queue serves smaller numeric priority keys first and compares equal priorities by an increasing arrival counter, also smallest first. If two tasks have equal priority, in what order are they served?
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 36

answer.text: FIFO among equal priorities: the task that arrived earlier is served first.
answer.explanation: The priority comparison ties, so the specified comparator proceeds to the arrival counter. An increasing counter gives the earlier arrival the smaller secondary key, causing it to be removed first. Equal-priority tasks are therefore served FIFO under this stable policy. That result follows from the explicitly chosen tie rule; an ordinary priority queue without a stability or comparator rule would not inherently guarantee arrival-order service.

evidence.quote: Arrays and lists can also implement priority queues: an unordered sequence gives cheap insertion but linear extremum removal; an ordered sequence reverses that tradeoff. Equal priorities have no inherent FIFO guarantee. If stable service is required, compare (priority, arrival_counter). Choose the priority direction and tie rule before tracing.

questions.stem: What causes queue underflow and what does it indicate?

answer.text: Dequeue on an empty queue causes underflow.
answer.explanation: DSA11 defines underflow as attempted removal from empty storage; DSA15’s count convention detects empty using size==0. This indicates that no item exists to return, not that the array is full or that an ordinary emptiness test itself failed.

evidence.quote: Overflow is an attempted insertion into full storage; underflow is an attempted removal from empty storage. Merely checking isEmpty does not underflow.

A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.

questions.stem: Name three real-world applications of stacks.

sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 38

answer.text: Runtime call frames, undo/redo history, and string or sequence reversal.
answer.explanation: DSA12 gives nested calls latest-first returns, moving latest actions between undo and redo stacks, and reversing input by pushing then popping. Each example uses the same latest-pending-item discipline. A new edit after undo normally clears redo history.

evidence.quote: Calls nest on a runtime stack; the latest call returns first. Bracket matching pushes opening brackets and matches each closing bracket against top. Reversal pushes input then pops it. Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back. A new edit after undo normally clears redo. DFS and backtracking use the same latest-pending-choice discipline.

questions.stem: What property must hold at every node of a Binary Search Tree?

answer.text: Every left-subtree key is smaller and every right-subtree key larger, for distinct keys.
answer.explanation: DSA19 imposes this invariant over entire subtrees at every node, not only immediate children. A descendant can satisfy its parent comparison yet violate an ancestor bound. Duplicate keys require an explicit count or placement policy instead of silently weakening the distinct-key rule.

evidence.quote: With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.

answer.explanation: DSA20 visits left subtree, node, then right subtree for inorder, and says BST inorder returns sorted keys. The supplied seven distinct keys therefore appear in increasing order even though the internal child shapes are not fully specified. Shape would matter to preorder or postorder.

evidence.quote: Preorder visits node,left,right; inorder left,node,right; postorder left,right,node. Apply recursively; null children do nothing. Inorder returns sorted keys only for a BST. Preorder supports copying, postorder supports deleting children before parents, and level order uses a FIFO queue.

With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.

questions.stem: When deleting a BST node with two children, what are the two valid replacement choices?
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 41

answer.explanation: DSA21 identifies the maximum key in the left subtree and minimum key in the right subtree as valid replacement values. Copy one into the deleted node, then remove that value’s original node, which has at most one child. These preserve the subtree order invariant.

evidence.quote: A leaf can be detached by clearing its parent link. For one child, make the parent bypass the node and point to the child. For two children, copy the inorder predecessor (left-subtree maximum) or successor (right-subtree minimum), then delete that replacement from its original location. That second deletion has at most one child.

questions.stem: What is the time complexity of BST search in the best case vs worst case?
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 42

answer.text: Best successful search Θ(1); arbitrary BST worst Θ(n), balanced worst Θ(log n).
answer.explanation: DSA19 gives a constant root hit and O(height) search. A chain has linear height, producing linear worst work; logarithmic height disciplines in DSA22 improve that worst bound. Calling every BST logarithmic would incorrectly assume balance.

evidence.quote: Search compares at each node and follows one child until equality or null. Insertion uses that same path to attach a new leaf. Operations cost O(height): logarithmic for balanced trees, linear for a chain. Best-case successful search is Theta(1), a root hit. An optimal BST minimizes expected search cost using access probabilities; constructing it is a different problem from searching it.

AVL balance factor is height(left)-height(right); every node must have factor -1,0 or 1. After insertion or deletion, update heights upward and rotate where necessary. LL imbalance needs a right rotation; RR needs left; LR rotates the left child left then the node right; RL is symmetric. Rotations preserve inorder key order.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between BFS and DFS graph traversal?
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 43

answer.text: BFS explores distance layers with FIFO; DFS finishes branches with a stack or recursion.
answer.explanation: DSA41 enqueues discoveries in layer order, while DSA42 resumes the latest unfinished branch before later neighbors. Both can traverse all reachable vertices, but their pending-work discipline and visitation order differ. BFS also has the unweighted minimum-edge guarantee.

evidence.quote: Mark the source when enqueuing it. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, examine its neighbours, and enqueue each unvisited neighbour while marking it. Store predecessor[v] when discovering v if a path must be reconstructed. FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers.

Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours. An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline. Marking prevents infinite repetition around graph cycles.

questions.stem: A directed graph has edges with direction; an undirected graph does not. Give one real-world example of each.
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 44

answer.text: Directed: following accounts; undirected: a mutual friendship relationship.
answer.explanation: DSA40 gives following as directed because u following v need not imply v following u. It gives mutual friendship as undirected, representing a symmetric connection. The examples concern relation semantics rather than whether lines happen to be drawn with arrows.

evidence.quote: A graph has vertices V and edges E. Directed edges distinguish u→v from v→u; undirected edges represent two-way relationships. Following accounts is directed; a mutual friendship relation is undirected. Weighted edges carry costs; unweighted shortest-path questions count edges. DAG expands to directed acyclic graph. Trees are connected acyclic graphs, although graph data structures may also contain cycles.

questions.stem: Why is a dense graph more computationally expensive to process than a sparse graph?
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 45

answer.text: Edge-processing algorithms do more work when E is larger.
answer.explanation: DSA40 says dense simple graphs approach quadratic edge counts and adjacency lists use Θ(V+E) space. Traversals or algorithms inspecting every edge therefore require more work as density increases. This is not universal: a vertex-only operation need not inspect edges.

evidence.quote: A matrix uses Theta(V²) space and constant edge lookup. Adjacency lists use Theta(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours. Dense simple graphs approach quadratic edge counts. Examining every edge costs more on denser graphs; vertex-only operations need not inspect every edge.

BFS finds minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary minimum-weight paths. With adjacency lists it costs O(V+E); scanning a matrix costs O(V²). To traverse a disconnected graph, restart from each unvisited vertex. Neighbour order affects tied traversal order but not minimum distances.

questions.stem: In a full binary tree, every node has either 0 or 2 children. How does this differ from a complete binary tree?
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 46

answer.text: Full restricts each node to zero or two children; complete restricts level filling.
answer.explanation: DSA18 defines full by each node’s child count and complete by filled earlier levels plus left-filled final level. Those are distinct conditions: completeness can allow one child at the boundary, while fullness alone need not keep every level filled.

evidence.quote: Binary means at most two children. Full means each node has zero or two children. Complete means all earlier levels are filled and the last fills from left. Perfect means all leaves share a level and every internal node has two children. Balanced means height stays logarithmic under a stated rule; it does not require a perfect shape.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a weighted graph from an unweighted graph, and when would you prefer weighted?
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 47

answer.text: Weighted edges carry differing costs; use them when edge costs matter.
answer.explanation: DSA40 assigns costs to weighted edges and says unweighted shortest-path questions count edges. Distances or travel costs can therefore justify weights when fewer edges is not the true objective. DSA43 then distinguishes weighted shortest paths from unweighted BFS.

evidence.quote: A graph has vertices V and edges E. Directed edges distinguish u→v from v→u; undirected edges represent two-way relationships. Following accounts is directed; a mutual friendship relation is undirected. Weighted edges carry costs; unweighted shortest-path questions count edges. DAG expands to directed acyclic graph. Trees are connected acyclic graphs, although graph data structures may also contain cycles.

For nonnegative weights, standard Dijkstra initializes source distance zero and others infinity, repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with smallest distance, and relaxes each outgoing edge: dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w(u,v)). A min-priority queue supports the next choice. BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.

questions.stem: If a BST receives keys in sorted order (1,2,3,4,5), what shape does the tree take and what is the search complexity?
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 48

answer.text: An ordinary unbalanced insertion forms a right chain; worst search is Θ(n).
answer.explanation: DSA19 explicitly traces sorted insertion 1,2,3,4,5 into a right chain. Each new larger key follows right links to the tail, making the height linear. Worst search follows that chain, while a root hit remains constant. Balanced insertion would rotate and is a different assumption.

evidence.quote: Search compares at each node and follows one child until equality or null. Insertion uses that same path to attach a new leaf. Operations cost O(height): logarithmic for balanced trees, linear for a chain. Best-case successful search is Theta(1), a root hit. An optimal BST minimizes expected search cost using access probabilities; constructing it is a different problem from searching it.
Sorted insertions 1,2,3,4,5 instead form a right chain.

questions.stem: When would you choose a linked list over an array? Give a specific scenario.
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 1

answer.text: Choose links for frequent known-location updates, such as a doubly linked history cursor.
answer.explanation: DSA10 gives browser history with a doubly linked cursor as an application. With references to current insertion or removal positions, link changes avoid shifting an array’s later elements; arbitrary positional lookup can still be linear. This concrete scenario supports the choice without claiming universal superiority.

evidence.quote: Lists suit changing sequences when references to insertion positions are already available. Finding a position is still linear. Lists can hold polynomial terms (coefficient, exponent), directory or block links, child lists in nonbinary trees, and hash chains. Browser history can use a doubly linked cursor. A playlist may be circular; airline seat lookup requires a specified seat-record model, not an automatic linked-list answer.

A fixed array has a chosen capacity; the choice need not occur at compile time. A resizable array allocates a larger block and copies when needed. Inserting in the middle shifts later elements, so it costs linear time. Appending into spare capacity is constant; a resizing append can be linear, though repeated geometric growth gives amortized constant append cost.

questions.stem: How does a stack differ from a queue? Give an application for each.
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 2

answer.text: Stack: LIFO for undo; queue: FIFO for equal-priority printer jobs.
answer.explanation: DSA11 gives latest-first stack service and DSA12 applies it to undoing the latest edit. DSA14 gives arrival-order queues for equal-priority printing. Both ADTs may use arrays or nodes; their service order, not that representation, is the distinction.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].

FIFO suits equal-priority printer jobs, shared-resource waiting, asynchronous buffers and level-order exploration. A play sequence can also use a queue. Distinguish airline seat records from waiting requests; an application name alone does not force one representation.
Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back.

questions.stem: Why is a balanced BST (like AVL) preferred over a regular BST? Explain the worst-case scenario.
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 3

answer.text: Balance prevents linear-height chains and guarantees logarithmic worst search.
answer.explanation: DSA22 maintains AVL balance factors through rotations that preserve inorder. DSA19 shows ordinary sorted insertion producing a chain, where a search can traverse all nodes. Maintaining logarithmic height prevents that worst degradation, though root-hit best time remains constant.

evidence.quote: AVL balance factor is height(left)-height(right); every node must have factor -1,0 or 1. After insertion or deletion, update heights upward and rotate where necessary. LL imbalance needs a right rotation; RR needs left; LR rotates the left child left then the node right; RL is symmetric. Rotations preserve inorder key order.

Search compares at each node and follows one child until equality or null. Insertion uses that same path to attach a new leaf. Operations cost O(height): logarithmic for balanced trees, linear for a chain. Best-case successful search is Theta(1), a root hit. An optimal BST minimizes expected search cost using access probabilities; constructing it is a different problem from searching it.

questions.stem: What is a hash collision? Name two methods to resolve collisions and compare them.
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 4

answer.text: A collision maps different keys to one home address; compare chaining and open addressing.
answer.explanation: DSA26 stores colliding entries in bucket lists for chaining, whereas open addressing probes other array slots. Chaining uses link or bucket overhead and expected O(1+α) work; probing keeps entries inside the table and requires careful load and deletion policies. Neither prevents all collisions.

evidence.quote: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.

Linear probing tries (h(k)+j)%m. For size 7 and keys 10,17,24, all home addresses are 3 and occupied positions become 3,4,5. Quadratic probing changes the step; double hashing uses h1(k)+j h2(k), modulo m, with a step relatively prime to m to cover all slots. Neither method guarantees no collisions. Deletion needs tombstones or reinsertion so searches do not stop prematurely.

questions.stem: What is the difference between BFS and DFS? Which finds the shortest path?
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 5
Algorithm Design & Analysis review questions · Question 4

answer.text: BFS uses FIFO layers and finds shortest unweighted paths; DFS uses branch-first stack order.
answer.explanation: DSA41 guarantees minimum-edge paths for BFS on unweighted graphs. DSA42 says DFS paths are reachability witnesses but need not be shortest. Differing edge weights require an appropriate weighted-path algorithm, such as Dijkstra under nonnegative weights.

evidence.quote: BFS finds minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary minimum-weight paths. With adjacency lists it costs O(V+E); scanning a matrix costs O(V²). To traverse a disconnected graph, restart from each unvisited vertex. Neighbour order affects tied traversal order but not minimum distances.

Using the same graph and alphabetical neighbours, recursive DFS can discover A,B,D,C. Its path is a valid reachability witness but not necessarily shortest. Adjacency-list cost is O(V+E), with O(V) visited state and possible stack depth. DFS supports cycle and connectivity analysis; a directed cycle test distinguishes active recursion vertices from already completed ones.
BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.

questions.stem: A text editor needs to implement multi-level undo. Which data structure is most appropriate and why?
questions.hint: Use the cited invariant or operation rule, state its assumptions, and trace a small case to justify the result.
sources: Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 6

answer.text: Use an undo stack, with a second redo stack if needed.
answer.explanation: DSA12 moves the latest action from undo to redo and reverses that movement for redo. Pushing each new edit and popping for undo naturally matches the most-recent-edit-first requirement. A new edit after undo normally clears redo history.

evidence.quote: Calls nest on a runtime stack; the latest call returns first. Bracket matching pushes opening brackets and matches each closing bracket against top. Reversal pushes input then pops it. Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back. A new edit after undo normally clears redo. DFS and backtracking use the same latest-pending-choice discipline.

Inorder returns sorted keys only for a BST.
Preorder supports copying, postorder supports deleting children before parents, and level order uses a FIFO queue.
For root 4, children 2 and 6, and leaves 1,3,5,7: preorder is 4,2,1,3,6,5,7; inorder is 1,2,3,4,5,6,7; postorder is 1,3,2,5,7,6,4.
Level order is 4,2,6,1,3,5,7.
Randomized visitation is possible; it is simply not one of these standard named depth-first orders.
Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: BST deletion preserves every subtree restriction

blocks.text: A leaf can be detached by clearing its parent link.
For one child, make the parent bypass the node and point to the child.
For two children, copy the inorder predecessor (left-subtree maximum) or successor (right-subtree minimum), then delete that replacement from its original location.
That second deletion has at most one child.
Deletion by merging is another approach.
Promote the right subtree and attach the entire old left subtree to the minimum node in the promoted right subtree; or use the symmetric left promotion.
Update root itself when deleting root.
Copying values and reconnecting subtrees can yield different valid shapes, so a trace must name its deletion method.
Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: Balanced trees prevent the sorted-input chain

blocks.text: AVL balance factor is height(left)-height(right); every node must have factor -1,0 or 1.
After insertion or deletion, update heights upward and rotate where necessary.
LL imbalance needs a right rotation; RR needs left; LR rotates the left child left then the node right; RL is symmetric.
Rotations preserve inorder key order.
Inserting 30,20,10 triggers LL repair: 20 becomes root with children 10,30.
Red-black colouring rules provide another logarithmic-height discipline.
Both prevent linear worst-case search; balanced trees also support ordered ranges unlike ordinary hashing.
Sedgewick and Wayne: Balanced Search Trees

notes.title: A heap combines completeness with a weaker ordering

blocks.text: A binary max-heap is complete with each parent at least its children; a min-heap reverses this order.
Unlike BSTs, heaps do not order entire subtrees.
The root is maximum.
If all keys are distinct, the second largest is a root child.
With duplicate maxima, the second largest distinct value may be deeper: [9,9,9,8,7,6,5] is a valid max-heap and that value is 8 at index 3.
The minimum may be any leaf, requiring linear worst-case scanning.
Zero-based array representation: root index 0, left=2i+1, right=2i+2, parent=floor((i-1)/2) for i>0.
One-based representation uses children 2i,2i+1 and parent floor(i/2).
A child exists only if its index is inside the current heap size.
Exam trap

items.text: The right-child formula 2i+1 assumes one-based indexing. For zero-based indexing with the root at index 0, the right-child formula is 2i+2.

blocks.text: Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: Restore a heap after insertion or removal

blocks.text: Insert at the next complete-tree position and swap upward while parent order is violated.
To remove the root, move the final element to root, reduce heap size, then swap downward with the more dominant child until order holds.
Each path has logarithmic length.
Building bottom-up by sinking internal nodes takes linear total time; repeated independent insertions give an O(n log n) construction bound.
Work it through

items.text: Max-heap [10,8,6,2,1,4,5]: remove 10, move 5 to root and sink, giving [8,5,6,2,1,4]. Remove 8, move 4 up then exchange with 6: [6,5,4,2,1].

blocks.text: Data Structure and Algorithms module
Sedgewick and Wayne: Priority Queues

notes.title: Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

blocks.text: Direct addressing reserves a position for every possible key in a finite universe U, costing Theta(|U|) slots.
A hash table uses h(key) in 0..m-1 and stores only actual entries plus bucket capacity.
With h(k)=k mod 6, key 36 has home address 0; collisions may move its final storage position.
Determinism means repeated equal keys get the same address for the chosen function.
Uniformity means expected keys spread evenly.
Universal hashing chooses one function randomly from a suitable family for the table, independently of a fixed key set; it does not choose a fresh unrelated function for each lookup.
Random choice controls collision probability, not a promise of zero collisions.
MIT 6.006: Recitation4 Hashing

notes.title: Resolve collisions and watch the load factor

blocks.text: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list.
Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases.
Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.
Linear probing tries (h(k)+j)%m. For size 7 and keys 10,17,24, all home addresses are 3 and occupied positions become 3,4,5.
Quadratic probing changes the step; double hashing uses h1(k)+j h2(k), modulo m, with a step relatively prime to m to cover all slots.
Neither method guarantees no collisions.
Deletion needs tombstones or reinsertion so searches do not stop prematurely.
At h(k)=3 in a seven-slot linear-probing table, addresses wrap 3,4,5,6,0,1,2.
A home address is not guaranteed to remain the final slot.
Sedgewick and Wayne: Hash Tables

notes.title: Maps, sets and caches specify different contracts

blocks.text: A map associates unique keys with values; different keys may share values, and entries can be traversed.
A set forbids duplicate elements.
Null and iteration-order policies depend on implementation.
Lists preserve positions and generally allow duplicates; Java LinkedList also permits null.
A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering.
A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list.
Move a hit to the recent end and evict the least-recent end when full.
No storage structure is universally best without operation and policy requirements.
Oracle Java SE 21: Map
Oracle Java SE 21: Set
Oracle Java SE 21: LinkedList
Oracle Java SE 21: LinkedHashMap

notes.title: Linear search: a scan with an early stop

blocks.text: Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted.
Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too.
A first-element match costs Theta(1).
An absent target or last-position match needs n comparisons, giving Theta(n) worst time.
Uniformly likely successful positions average (n+1)/2 comparisons, still linear.
For a single unsorted query, sorting first is rarely justified.
Small lists may favour scanning because setup matters.
Sorting does not avoid examining all values for mean, variance or arbitrary parity counts.
Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

blocks.text: On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1.
Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2.
Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1.
Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi.
Reverse comparisons for descending order.
Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.
Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million.
Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth.
Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time.
Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.
Work it through

items.text: Find 19 in [11,13,15,17,19,21]: mid=2 gives 15; search indices 3..5; mid=4 gives 19. Binary debugging needs an ordered good/bad boundary, not arbitrary fault locations.

blocks.text: Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: Search variants need their own assumptions

blocks.text: Interpolation search estimates the index from numeric values: lo+(hi-lo)×(key-A[lo])/(A[hi]-A[lo]), rounded to a valid index.
Guard equal endpoints and out-of-range targets.
On sorted, suitably uniform data its expected probes can be O(log log n); pathological distributions can require linear time.
Binary search gives a logarithmic worst bound without that distribution assumption.
Sorted-array ternary search compares two split points and keeps the relevant third, still logarithmic.
Jump search probes block boundaries then scans within a block.
Regular intervals could mean unit-step scanning or larger jumps.
Interpolation also needs sortedness, so prerequisite questions can overlap binary search.
University of Waterloo, Douglas Harder: Interpolation Search
University of Massachusetts: Running Time lecture
University of Waterloo, Douglas Harder: Jump Search

notes.title: Compare sorting rules, not just algorithm names

blocks.text: Stable sorting preserves the input order of equal keys.
An in-place element algorithm uses a fixed amount of extra element storage; a recursive call stack may still matter when total auxiliary space is requested.
There is no single algorithm identified by stable or in-place alone.
State the implementation, input case and resource being compared.

rows: n log n / n log n / n²
stack usually log n average, n worst; unstable
n log n in all cases
O(n log n) bound in all cases

blocks.text: Exam trap

items.text: Big-O bounds can overlap. n log(n²)=2n log n, so it has the same growth as n log n, unlike n(log n)².

blocks.text: Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: Bubble sort: complete adjacent passes

blocks.text: For ascending order, compare each adjacent pair and swap only when left>right.
The largest remaining value moves to the final unsorted position after one left-to-right pass.
Shrink the next pass by one position.
Quadratic worst/average work comes from up to n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons.
Early stopping makes a sorted input linear: one no-swap pass finishes.
A fixed pass schedule stays quadratic.
Strict swaps preserve equal-key order.
Cocktail sort runs bubble passes in both directions and is stable with strict swaps.
Work it through
Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons

blocks.text: At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i].
There are n-1 meaningful placements and n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of initial order.
At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed.
A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls.
Selection suits expensive record moves with cheap key comparisons, not every large dataset.
It is unstable: exchanging first 2a with 1 in [2a,2b,1] gives [1,2b,2a].
Constant extra element storage is shared by several sorts.
Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: Insertion sort: extend a sorted prefix

blocks.text: Begin with the first element already sorted.
For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap.
That gives n-1 insertion passes.
On sorted input each pass needs one ordering check and no shifts: linear time.
Reverse order causes 1+2+…+(n-1) shifts: quadratic time.
Few inversions mean few shifts, favouring insertion for nearly sorted or small arrays.
Shift only strictly larger keys for stability.
A linked implementation saves array shifts but still must locate each insertion position.
Work it through

items.text: Insert 2 into prefix [1,4,7]: save 2, move 7 then 4 right, and write 2 after 1. The sorted prefix becomes [1,2,4,7].

blocks.text: Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: Shell sort: insertion across decreasing gaps

blocks.text: Choose a sequence of positive gaps ending at 1.
For each gap h, insertion-sort each subsequence of positions h apart.
The final h=1 pass finishes ordinary sorting after earlier long moves have reduced disorder.
An h-sorted array satisfies A[j]≤A[j+h] wherever both indices exist.
The O(n^(3/2)) bound depends on gaps; Knuth increments 1,4,13,… have that worst order.
Shell sort is generally unstable because distant moves can reorder ties; extra element storage is constant.
Work it through

items.text: For [5,4,3,2,1], gap 3 sorts positions (0,3) and (1,4), giving [2,1,3,5,4]. Gap 1 then produces [1,2,3,4,5].

blocks.text: Data Structure and Algorithms module
Sedgewick and Wayne: Shell.java

notes.title: Quicksort: separate partition guarantees from exact traces

blocks.text: Choose a pivot, partition, then recursively sort the pieces.
Balanced partitions give n log n work; repeated extreme pivots sum n+(n-1)+… to quadratic work.
Expected n log n needs an input/random-pivot model.
Random and median-of-three choices have different tradeoffs; neither is universally best.
In the ten-distinct-value example, a final pivot 5 has five smaller values before it and four larger after it.
Internal orders depend on the partition algorithm; several candidate arrays can satisfy the invariant.
State the algorithm before predicting one exact array.
Quicksort normally rearranges in the same array but recursive storage can be linear in the worst case.
Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

blocks.text: Split into halves, sort them, then merge by advancing the smaller current front.
With left-first tie handling, equal keys retain order.
Ordinary array merging needs a linear auxiliary buffer.
There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.
Top-down mergesort recurses; bottom-up merges runs of widths 1,2,4,… iteratively.
In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant.
Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory.
External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O. Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons.
Data Structure and Algorithms module
Virginia Tech OpenDSA: External Sorting

notes.title: Heapsort: repeatedly place the extreme at the end

blocks.text: For ascending in-place heapsort, build a max-heap over the array.
Exchange root with the final active element, shrink the active heap, and sink the new root.
The removed maximum now belongs in the sorted suffix.
Repeat until one active item remains.
Building with bottom-up sinking is linear; repeated extraction gives O(n log n) worst time.
Iterative sinking needs constant auxiliary storage.
The method is generally unstable because long root-to-end exchanges can reorder equal keys.
It is not uniquely the method for sorting by priorities: any comparison sort can compare a priority field.
Heap extraction is its distinctive mechanism.
Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: Radix sorting uses key digits, not arbitrary magic

blocks.text: LSD radix sorting handles fixed-width digit keys by stably sorting least-significant digit first, then moving left.
Stable intermediate passes preserve the ordering already established by less-significant digits.
With d digits and radix r, counting-based passes take O(d(n+r)) time and O(n+r) auxiliary storage.
MSD begins at leading digits and subdivides equal-prefix groups.
Strings are lexicographically comparable.
Radix methods require accessible digits and length/signed-value conventions, not arbitrary unstructured keys.
Large radix, long keys or small n may favour comparison sorting.
Sedgewick and Wayne: LSD.java

notes.title: Graphs: represent the relationships you actually need

blocks.text: A graph has vertices V and edges E. Directed edges distinguish u→v from v→u; undirected edges represent two-way relationships.
Following accounts is directed; a mutual friendship relation is undirected.
Weighted edges carry costs; unweighted shortest-path questions count edges.
DAG expands to directed acyclic graph.
Trees are connected acyclic graphs, although graph data structures may also contain cycles.
A matrix uses Theta(V²) space and constant edge lookup.
Adjacency lists use Theta(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours.
Dense simple graphs approach quadratic edge counts.
Examining every edge costs more on denser graphs; vertex-only operations need not inspect every edge.
Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: BFS: discover one distance layer at a time

blocks.text: Mark the source when enqueuing it.
Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, examine its neighbours, and enqueue each unvisited neighbour while marking it.
Store predecessor[v] when discovering v if a path must be reconstructed.
FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers.
BFS finds minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary minimum-weight paths.
With adjacency lists it costs O(V+E); scanning a matrix costs O(V²).
To traverse a disconnected graph, restart from each unvisited vertex.
Neighbour order affects tied traversal order but not minimum distances.
Work it through

items.text: Edges A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D; alphabetical neighbours: queue [A] → [B,C] → [C,D] → [D] → []. Discovery order A,B,C,D; D has distance two.

blocks.text: Sedgewick and Wayne: Undirected Graphs

notes.title: DFS: finish a branch before returning

blocks.text: Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours.
An explicit stack can store pending work instead.
Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline.
Marking prevents infinite repetition around graph cycles.
Using the same graph and alphabetical neighbours, recursive DFS can discover A,B,D,C. Its path is a valid reachability witness but not necessarily shortest.
Adjacency-list cost is O(V+E), with O(V) visited state and possible stack depth.
DFS supports cycle and connectivity analysis; a directed cycle test distinguishes active recursion vertices from already completed ones.
Data Structure and Algorithms module

notes.title: Shortest paths and spanning trees solve different objectives

blocks.text: For nonnegative weights, standard Dijkstra initializes source distance zero and others infinity, repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with smallest distance, and relaxes each outgoing edge: dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w(u,v)).
A min-priority queue supports the next choice.
BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.
An MST minimizes the total cost of connecting all vertices of a connected undirected weighted graph.
Prim adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex.
Kruskal processes edges by increasing weight and rejects those joining vertices already connected.
An MST need not give shortest source-to-vertex routes, and equal weights can permit several MSTs.
Work it through

items.text: Triangle weights AB=1, BC=2, AC=10: Prim or Kruskal selects AB,BC, total 3. Dijkstra from A gets B=1 and improves C from 10 to 3 through B.

blocks.text: Sedgewick and Wayne: Shortest Paths

notes.title: Recognize two other tested algorithms through their rules

blocks.text: Kadane’s algorithm finds a contiguous maximum-sum subarray.
For a required nonempty answer, initialize ending=best=A[0]; update ending=max(x,ending+x), then best=max(best,ending).
It is linear time with constant working storage.
Initializing best=0 instead silently allows an empty answer and fails the nonempty all-negative case.
Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) finds a pattern inside text.
Preprocess the pattern’s longest proper prefix that is also a suffix.
After mismatch, fall back using those prefix lengths rather than restarting comparisons from the beginning; the text pointer need not move backward.
Pattern preprocessing plus scanning takes O(pattern length+text length).
Work it through

items.text: For [-2,3,-1,4,-5], Kadane ending values are -2,3,2,6,1, so best is 6 from [3,-1,4]. Pattern ABAB has prefix lengths [0,0,1,2].

Jayadev Misra, University of Texas: Knuth-Morris-Pratt Algorithm

notes.title: State trace data and representation assumptions

blocks.text: A trace needs the complete operation sequence, initial state, capacity and output orientation.
State these assumptions before calculating.
Evaluate all choices against the rules; a selected answer does not make other valid choices false.
Specify whether a question asks which structure can implement something or which is best under stated costs.
ADTs do not force one representation, and serial-access memory is not inherently LIFO.
A heap file is an unordered database record file, unrelated to a binary heap: insertion uses available space, scanning can find records, and ordered output requires sorting or an index.
It need not insert at the beginning.
Data Structure and Algorithms module
UC Berkeley CS186: Disk and Files

notes.title: Best, average and worst compare equal-size inputs

blocks.text: Fix the input size before comparing cases. Best-case cost is the minimum resource use over legal inputs of that size; worst-case cost is the maximum. Average-case cost averages costs using a stated input distribution. These three input-case functions can each be described using upper, lower or tight asymptotic bounds; the case name does not select the bound notation.

For successful binary search with all stored positions equally likely, average probes have order Theta(log n). The probe decisions form a binary tree: only a bounded number of positions occur in shallow levels, while a constant fraction require logarithmic depth. Interval halving also gives the logarithmic upper bound. A distribution concentrating on an immediate midpoint hit would give a different average.
NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures — Best case
NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures — Worst case
NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures — Average case
Sedgewick and Wayne — Algorithms, binary-search symbol-table average costs

notes.title: Queues for deferred interrupt work

blocks.text: An interrupt service routine may need to record work quickly and defer its completion. Operating systems can queue that deferred work for later processing; Windows deferred procedure calls are one concrete example. This is a queue application, but it does not imply that every interrupt system uses a single FIFO service policy.
Microsoft — Introduction to DPC objects

notes.title: Linked nodes and multiway tree branching

blocks.text: A linked binary-tree node stores a payload and two child pointers, one for the left child and one for the right child. A null child pointer means that child is absent; a root pointer gives access to the whole tree. In a dynamically allocated version, insertion can allocate a node and attach it through the appropriate child link.

A B-tree is a balanced multiway search tree. Its allowed branching factor can exceed two, so a general B-tree is not the binary-tree family. Balanced describes a height discipline; it does not by itself restrict every node to two children.
Data Structure and Algorithms module · page 9

notes.title: Recognize recursive divide-and-conquer structure

blocks.text: Divide and conquer reduces a problem to smaller instances of the same kind, solves the required smaller instances and obtains the original result from them. Mergesort recursively sorts two halves and merges; quicksort partitions and recursively sorts the resulting ranges. This course also classifies binary search as divide and conquer: an ordered comparison selects the only half that can contain the target. This is different from simply repeating adjacent swaps, choosing successive minima, or making stable LSD digit passes.

Practise without answer keys, then justify every choice using an invariant or a short calculation.
